title: He Found India at Auckland Diwali; a Decade Later He Runs the Festival
excerpt: Festival event manager Arnav Taode now leads the free BNZ Auckland Diwali Festival, returning to Aotea Square on October 31 and November 1 with stages, vegetarian food and fireworks.
body:
• The BNZ Auckland Diwali Festival returns free to Aotea Square and Queen Street on Saturday, October 31 and Sunday, November 1, 2026, from midday to about 9pm, Auckland Council says.
  • Tātaki Auckland Unlimited festival event manager Arnav Taode — profiled by Awaaz as a man who found a piece of India at the festival and, a decade later, is running it — now leads the event.
  • Expect multiple stages of Indian music and dance, vegetarian food, workshops, a rangoli competition, and Sunday fireworks at about 8:50pm.
  • Reader utility: entry is free; Te Waihorotiu Station is a five-minute walk from Aotea Square, and Auckland Transport warns of road closures and detours after 8pm.

A decade after he first found a piece of India at Auckland's Diwali festival, Arnav Taode is running it. That is the arc Awaaz traced in its profile of the Tātaki Auckland Unlimited festival event manager, and it is now the human story behind the BNZ Auckland Diwali Festival, which returns to central Auckland on Saturday, October 31 and Sunday, November 1, 2026.

The festival, launched in 2002 and described by Auckland Council as one of the largest Diwali celebrations in the Southern Hemisphere, takes over Aotea Square, Queen Street, Rutland Street and surrounding venues. Entry is free, and the programme runs from midday to 9pm on Saturday and to about 9:10pm on Sunday.

The Manager's Own Festival

Taode's public message for 2026 is about connection. In the council's festival announcement he said Diwali has always been a time when families and communities come together, and that the same sense of connection sits at the heart of the Auckland festival. He added that Auckland's Indian communities celebrate Diwali in many different ways, and the festival gives them a platform to share their culture with the whole city.

"Diwali has always been a joyful time when families and communities come together."

— Arnav Taode, Festival Event Manager, Tātaki Auckland Unlimited

That framing matters for a migrant-led festival. For a newcomer, a public Diwali in Aotea Square is often the first place a new city feels like home — familiar food, music and rituals in the main square, at civic scale. A manager who arrived at the festival as an audience member brings that memory into programming choices about stages, food and family space.

What Is On in 2026

Auckland Council says traditional and contemporary Indian performances will run across multiple stages, alongside vegetarian food and sweet treats for purchase, and stalls selling Indian arts and crafts, fashion, jewellery and henna. Returning favourites include the Chalk It Up Rangoli Competition, yoga and meditation sessions, and activities for children and families.

New and expanded elements include an Indian art exhibition with India-based Baaya Design, workshops in a calmer Living Arts Chillout Space at Aotea Centre, a free Indian Cinema Showcase, and a free three-hour Indian classical music concert in the Concert Chamber at Auckland Town Hall. The Sky Tower, Auckland Art Gallery, Auckland War Memorial Museum and Auckland Harbour Bridge will be lit in fuchsia and orange, with projection mapping at Auckland Town Hall and Te Waihorotiu Station. Sunday's fireworks are expected at about 8:50pm.

Getting There

Plan the trip before you go. Auckland Transport's event page says frequent trains run to Te Waihorotiu Station, a five-minute walk from Aotea Square, with extra capacity on key lines. The Downtown Ferry Terminal is about a 15-minute walk away. Auckland Transport warns that parking will be limited, some bus routes will be detoured after 8pm because of road closures, and crowds between the station and the square will be heavy.

Children aged 5 to 15 travel free on weekends with a registered AT HOP card, and children under 5 travel free with a paying passenger, Auckland Transport says. Standard fares otherwise apply, paid by AT HOP card, contactless card or phone.

Why It Matters Beyond Auckland

The festival is also part of 100 Years of Unity Through Sport, a year-long national programme marking a century of connections between India and New Zealand. For the wider diaspora, Taode's story is the point: public festivals do not just entertain migrants, they recruit them — first as homesick visitors, then as volunteers, producers and, eventually, the people running the show.
